shower.thought: # Shower Thoughts
Nostalgia is just your brain playing the highlights reel of a time you were too busy living to actually enjoy.
You've probably had the same thought as someone on the other side of the world at the exact same moment, and you'll never know it.
The moment you stop being afraid of silence is the moment you discover who you actually are.
Everyone assumes they're the main character, which means we're all living in a world of side characters who think they're starring in their own movie.
You can't remember most of your life, which means most of your life technically didn't happen to the person you are now.
The people who say "money doesn't matter" either have enough of it or not enough of it to think clearly about it.
We call it "falling" asleep but "waking up," as if sleep is an accident and consciousness is the recovery.
Your phone knows more about your future than you do.
The scariest thing about getting older isn't aging — it's realizing how little time you actually wasted on things that mattered.
Compliments about things you can't change (looks, height, voice) feel better than compliments about things you worked for, which says something depressing about us.
You're nostalgic for a version of your life that never actually existed the way you remember it.
Every conversation you have is a collaboration on deciding what reality is, and most people don't realize they're negotiating.
The internet gave everyone a platform and somehow that made most people's voices quieter.
You only feel like an impostor in areas where you care about being competent.
Boredom is just your brain telling you it's run out of new patterns to find in your current situation.
The hardest part of growing up isn't becoming an adult — it's accepting that other people aren't growing at the same speed you are.
We fear death but spend most of our lives doing things that feel like slow practice runs at it.
You don't actually want to be happy all the time; you just want to feel like your suffering means something.
The people who changed your life probably have no idea they did.

darkjoke.thought:
I told my girlfriend she was drawing her eyebrows too high.
She looked surprised.

My grandfather said, "Your generation is too reliant on technology."
I said, "Says the guy who needs a pacemaker to stay reliant on anything."

I tried meal prepping on Sunday.
By Wednesday I was eating sadness with a side of regret.

The doctor told me I have six months to live.
I said I couldn't pay the bill.
He said, "Okay, you have a year."

My dating profile says I'm "brutally honest."
Turns out women don't appreciate brutal without the honest part.

I asked my boss for a raise.
He said, "You're doing great, but let's wait until you're irreplaceable."
I've been irreplaceable for three years.

My therapist asked what my biggest fear was.
I said, "That I'll end up like you."

I went to a self-help seminar called "Living Your Best Life."
The instructor looked miserable.
I think I learned something.

My friend got sober and found Jesus.
I'm happy for him, but now he won't shut up about either one.

I told my son that life isn't fair.
He said, "I know, I saw your inheritance."

The gym trainer said, "No pain, no gain."
I said, "Great, I'm already in pain and making no gains."

My wife asked if I remembered the day we met.
I said, "Of course, it was the worst day of your life too."
She didn't laugh.

I'm not saying I'm lazy, but my autobiography is just a list of missed opportunities.
My editor said it was "too relatable" to publish.

My accountant asked why I had so many therapy sessions on my tax return.
I said, "Would you like me to list them chronologically or by effectiveness?"

I asked my friend how his marriage was going.
He said, "It's like a reality show, except nobody's watching and we can't afford to cancel it."

My doctor said I needed to cut back on caffeine.
I agreed, then realized I was the only thing keeping me functional.
We're working through it.

I went to my high school reunion.
Everyone asked what I was doing with my life.
I said, "Apparently, showing up to this."

My dad told me he was proud of me.
Then he asked for money.
I think he was practicing both emotions.

I asked my cat what she thought of my life choices.
She knocked my phone off the table.
Fair assessment.

My therapist said I should write down my feelings.
So I did.
Turns out my handwriting is as depressing as my thoughts.
